title: RAG Architecture Patterns
description: Naive RAG vs advanced RAG. Chunking strategies, reranking, hybrid search, and practical implementation patterns.

data.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from a simple 'search-then-generate' pipeline into a sophisticated ecosystem of retrieval strategies, ranking systems, and context-management techniques. Understanding these patterns is essential for building RAG systems that are accurate, fast, and reliable in production.

Naive RAG follows three simple steps: embed the user query, find the top-k most similar document chunks in a vector database, and stuff those chunks into an LLM prompt. It works for straightforward Q&A but degrades quickly with large document collections, ambiguous queries, or when retrieved chunks are only partially relevant.

data.text: Advanced RAG introduces multiple improvements over the baseline. These include hybrid search (combining vector and keyword search), query rewriting for better retrieval, reranking of retrieved chunks, and context compression to reduce token usage while preserving information density.

cards.title: Naive RAG
cards.description: Simple vector search and generation. Good for small, clean document collections.

cards.title: Advanced RAG
cards.description: Hybrid search + reranking + query transformation. Production-grade retrieval.

cards.title: Modular RAG
cards.description: Fully composable architecture with routing, multiple retrievers, and feedback loops.

data.text: How you split documents into retrievable chunks is one of the most impactful decisions in RAG. Fixed-size chunking is simple but often splits mid-sentence or mid-thought. Semantic chunking respects content boundaries. Recursive splitting uses a hierarchy of separators. The right strategy depends on your document structure and query patterns.

rows: Split every N characters with overlap
Can create too many tiny chunks
Try paragraph, then sentence, then word
Only works if document is well-structured

data.text: Hybrid search combines vector similarity search with traditional keyword (BM25) search. Vector search captures semantics, while keyword search captures exact matches. By fusing the two result sets — often with a Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) algorithm — you get better recall and precision than either method alone.

Most production RAG systems now use hybrid search. Pure vector search misses exact-match queries (product codes, legal references). Pure keyword search misses synonyms and paraphrases. Together, they cover both cases.

Reranking is a second-stage retrieval step. After the initial broad retrieval (e.g., top-50 chunks from hybrid search), a more powerful (but slower) cross-encoder model re-scores all candidates based on the exact query-chunk pair. Cross-encoders process query and chunk together, so they can judge true relevance rather than just embedding similarity.

data.title: Reranking in action
data.content:
User query: 'What is the refund policy for damaged goods?'

Step 1 - Initial retrieval (bi-encoder, fast):
- Chunk A: 'Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days' (score: 0.82)
- Chunk B: 'Damaged goods may be returned within 30 days for a full refund' (score: 0.79)
- Chunk C: 'Shipping costs are non-refundable' (score: 0.76)

Step 2 - Reranking (cross-encoder, precise):
- Chunk B moves to #1 (cross-encoder score: 0.95) — it actually answers the question
- Chunk A drops to #2 (score: 0.60) — it's about timing, not eligibility
- Chunk C drops to #3 (score: 0.20) — irrelevant

data.text: Retrieved chunks consume valuable context window space. If you retrieve 10 chunks of 500 tokens each, that's 5,000 tokens just for context — leaving less room for the actual conversation. Advanced RAG systems use context compression, max marginal relevance (MMR) for diversity, and dynamic top-k selection to balance information density with token budget.

data.title: Context management techniques:
items: Max Marginal Relevance (MMR) — balances relevance with diversity to avoid redundant chunks
Context compression — use an LLM to summarize chunks before injection
Dynamic top-k — adjust how many chunks you retrieve based on query complexity
Windowed retrieval — for multi-turn conversations, retrieve only relevant prior turns
Source attribution — preserve chunk IDs so the LLM can cite its sources

data.title: Production RAG checklist
points: Use semantic chunking or recursive splitting over fixed-size
Add a reranker as a second-stage step
Use MMR or diversity filters to avoid repetitive context
Track chunk relevance scores and retrieval precision
Monitor token usage per query to control costs
data.takeaway: The gap between naive RAG and production RAG isn't one feature — it's a layered architecture of retrieval, ranking, and context engineering.
